CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION

                What a Point of View Can Determine


                                  Flyxion

                        Independent Researcher

                              October 2026


                                 Abstract

Miranker and Zuckerman’s Dynamics of mental activity represents recurrent neu-
ral activity by circular set structures and transports threshold-network dynamics
into that representation. Under Aczel’s anti-foundation axiom each node of a
weighted network receives a set, its decoration, built from the decorations of the
nodes it connects to together with a well-founded label recording the active in-
coming weights. The authors show that, for ﬁnite graphs in which every node
starts an arrow, the label can be read back from the decoration, and that the volt-
age, histogram and decoration dynamics can then be carried into one another
at ﬁxed weights. They go on to interpret the decoration of a single distinguished
node, the thema, as a primary experience on which a consciousness operator acts.
   This essay separates three things the construction can be taken to show: that
a representation is lossless, that a projection of it is dynamically closed, and that
the projected object is an experience. The ﬁrst is established under stated struc-
tural restrictions, and what it recovers is the labeling on a ﬁxed graph, not the
graph. The second is a checkable condition, πS = Fπ, which asks whether states
that look the same from the projection also look the same after the system up-
dates. Whether it holds must be established for the network and distinguished
node under consideration, and the passage from a full decoration to the thema is
many-to-one, so the condition can fail where the representation is lossless. The
third requires an empirical bridge that the axioms do not supply, since the four
axioms for consciousness operators ﬁx a family of selection rules and nothing
that separates conscious from unconscious activity.
   Treating a point of view as a projection turns the question of subjectivity into
the question of when the viewpoint determines its own continuation. Where
closure holds, the thematic level is a dynamical system in its own right and can be
studied in its own terms. Where it fails, any description conﬁned to the viewpoint
depends on information the viewpoint does not contain. The same condition
applies to any mechanism that selects which features of a system to retain, and
it separates selection that is shown to be sufﬁcient for a task from selection that
merely happens to be.

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                      2



1. CIRCULAR STRUCTURE AND DECORATION

The construction begins with a point about what set membership can express. In ordi-
nary well-founded set theory, membership cannot circle back on itself: no set contains
itself, either directly or through a chain of memberships. Aczel’s anti-foundation ax-
iom [1] removes this restriction and in exchange guarantees that every directed graph
has a unique decoration, an assignment of a set to each node such that the elements
of the set at a node are exactly the sets assigned to its children. The simplest case
is the two-node graph with edges x →y and y →x, whose decoration satisﬁes
d(x) = {d(y)} and d(y) = {d(x)} and so describes mutual membership. Under anti-
foundation the unique decoration identiﬁes the two sets, so that d(x) = d(y) = q with
q = {q}, a set known as a Quine atom. Two nodes that are plainly distinct as nodes of
the graph denote the same set. A representation by membership structure therefore
preserves exactly the distinctions that membership structure can express and discards
the others. Labels can break the identiﬁcation: in the labeled equation introduced be-
low, two such nodes receive the same decoration only if their labels agree.

Miranker and Zuckerman [2, 3] apply this apparatus to recurrent networks by assign-
ing to each node a a set d(a), its decoration, satisfying what they call the M-Z equation

                          d(a) = { d(b) | a →b } ∪H(a),

where a →b denotes a directed edge and H(a) is a well-founded label encoding a
histogram of the active incoming synaptic weights. The ﬁrst part of the right-hand
side collects the decorations of the nodes that a connects to, and the second carries
local numerical information about activity. Because the network may contain cycles,
these equations cannot be evaluated by working backward from terminal nodes. They
must be solved together, which is what the anti-foundation axiom licenses. A pointed
graph decorated in this way pictures a set. The authors call such a picture a meme
and the set decorating its point the thema. The terms are technical and unrelated to
the popular sense of “meme.” A thema can be pictured by many different memes: the
foundations paper notes that an unbounded number of neural states and associated
graphs can share one and the same thema.

What this representation gains is a description of each node through its relations to
the rest of the network, with activity data built in. What it raises is the question that
organizes the rest of this essay: which distinctions survive a given representation, and
do the surviving distinctions sufﬁce to determine what happens next. The argument
proceeds from the representation itself to what can be recovered from it (Section 2),
to the dynamics transported through it (Section 3). It then turns to the closure condi-
tion for a projection (Section 4), before asking what that condition does and does not
license for the interpretation of the thema as experience (Sections 5 and 6).

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                      3



2. RECOVERABILITY

The dynamics paper’s most useful result for present purposes concerns recoverability
[3]. It introduces the selector

                  W(x) = { y ∈x | y is well-founded },


which keeps only the well-founded elements of a set. Under the restrictions the
authors impose in the dynamics paper, every node decoration is non-well-founded,
while the elements of the histogram labels are well-founded, the latter because a his-
togram is a ﬁnite set of pairs consisting of a weight and a positive multiplicity [2].
The two components of the decoration equation can then be separated, because W
discards the decorations contributed by neighboring nodes and retains the local label.
The result is
                            W(d(a)) = H(a),

so the histogram labels can be read back out of the encoding. The labels are not
the activity data itself, since a histogram already discards which presynaptic neurons
were active.

The restriction carries real weight and should be stated as part of the result.  If a
neighboring decoration were well-founded, W would retain it alongside the label and
the simple separation would fail. The recovery theorem is a property of a particular
class of decorated graphs, and the authors restrict their development to that class in
order to obtain it.

It is also worth being exact about what recovery establishes. That a label can be ex-
tracted from a decoration is a fact about the encoding.  It does not show that any
system consulted the label in producing a decision, used it appropriately, or retained
every distinction a later revision would need. Encoding, access, use, and sufﬁciency
are four separate questions, and the paper’s recovery result bears only on the ﬁrst.

Proposition 2.1 (Label recovery under separation). Let Ca = { d(b)  | a →b } and
suppose that every element of Ca is non-well-founded and every element of H(a) is well-
founded. Then W(d(a)) = H(a).

Proof. By the decoration equation, d(a) = Ca ∪H(a). Selecting the well-founded ele-
ments discards every element of Ca and keeps every element of H(a), so W(d(a)) =
H(a).


The dynamics paper does not assume the separation directly but obtains it from struc-
tural hypotheses. Its Deﬁnition 6.1 calls a multigraph non-well-founded when every
node is the starting point of an arrow, and Hypothesis 9.2 restricts attention to ﬁ-
nite graphs of this kind. Under that restriction every node decoration is non-well-
founded, and for any labeling by well-founded sets the labeling is recovered as the

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                      4



well-founded part of the decoration [3, Propositions 6.2, 6.3 and 9.3]. The proposition
above isolates the separation step inside that argument. The restriction is not idle: the
paper’s own example of a node with no outgoing arrow has a well-founded decora-
tion, and there the well-founded part picks up that decoration along with the label.
What is recovered is the labeling on a ﬁxed graph, not the graph itself.


3. TRANSPORTED DYNAMICS

The dynamics begin from the McCulloch–Pitts model of a binary threshold neuron
[2, 3]. The voltage of a neuron at the next step is

                         (                    )
                    vnew(a) = h ∑ w(p →a) vold(p) −θ   ,
                                                      p: p→a

where h is the Heaviside function, θ is a threshold, and the sum runs over the neurons
p that connect directly to a. Incoming weighted activity decides whether a neuron
ﬁres. The foundations paper pairs this with Hebb’s rule for weight change, so that
the complete model is a coupled system for voltages and weights; the dynamics pa-
per itself takes the synaptic weights to be time independent, so that the graph, the
weights and the threshold are parameters of every update it deﬁnes, and the same
convention is followed here [3, Section 7 and Remark 7.5]. The transported dynamics
therefore describe changing activity at ﬁxed connectivity, and not the coupled evolu-
tion of activity and plasticity. From the voltage update the dynamics paper builds
dynamics for the histograms, generalized to what it calls crops, and then for the dec-
orations.

Write AΓ for the transformation from labels to decorations and T for the update on
labels induced by the voltage update at ﬁxed weights. The induced update on deco-
rations is
                            S = AΓ T A−1Γ  .

On the relevant image, W supplies the inverse, which gives


                                d(t + 1) = AΓ T W d(t).


This is transport of dynamics through an invertible representation: recover the la-
bels, update them, and rebuild the decoration.  It shows that the set-based descrip-
tion evolves consistently with the underlying activity model, and nothing more. Nor
does the invertibility of the representation make the evolution reversible in time. The
threshold update can send distinct activity patterns to the same pattern, and a lossless
change of representation inherits that. Invertibility of the encoding and reversibility
of the process are different properties, and the paper establishes only the ﬁrst.

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                      5



4. THE CLOSURE CONDITION

Closure here means dynamical closure of a projection: whether the projected states
can be updated without reference to the full state they were drawn from.

Deﬁnition 4.1 (Dynamical closure of a projection). Let S update full states and let π
extract a projected state. A deterministic update F on projected states exists with

                          πS = Fπ


if and only if
                   π(µ1) = π(µ2) =⇒π(Sµ1) = π(Sµ2).

The projection π is then closed under S.

This is the congruence condition behind lumpability of Markov chains [4], bisimu-
lation quotients [5], and homomorphisms of dynamical systems in the coalgebraic
sense [6]. It is a requirement on a lossy projection, so invertibility is neither needed
nor assumed.

Remark 4.2. The representation is loop-sensitive, since a decoration encodes the struc-
ture reachable from its node, cycles included. What the thema can lose is of three
kinds. Nodes that are bisimilar in the associated membership graph, in which each el-
ement of a label counts as an additional child, receive the same decoration, so distinct
graphs whose membership structure unfolds identically from the point share a thema.
Bisimilarity here concerns membership structure, not the behavior of the network un-
der the update S. The labels record only multiplicities of active incoming weights,
so the identity of the active presynaptic neurons is not retained beyond those counts.
And nothing is recorded about parts of the network that cannot be reached from the
point along directed edges. A failure of closure therefore reﬂects missing information
of these kinds, and not a failure to register cycles.

The passage from the full decorated network to the thema is where the lossless equiv-
alences end. The foundations paper is explicit that the passage is many-to-one: many
graphs have a given set as the decoration of their point, and the neural states shar-
ing one thema are in principle unboundedly many [2]. There is a unique canonical
tree whose decoration is a given set, so the thema determines its pointed graph once
graphs are restricted to canonical trees, but not when arbitrary graphs are allowed.
Under Aczel’s theory two pointed graphs have the same decoration exactly when
they are bisimilar [1]. For labeled graphs the relevant graph is the expanded one in
which each element of a label is attached as an additional child, because the deco-
ration equation merges label elements with successor decorations: a terminal node
labeled {∅} and an unlabeled node with an edge to an unlabeled terminal node both
receive the decoration {∅}. The separation of well-founded labels from non-well-
founded successor decorations in Section 2 rules out this particular ambiguity. The

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                      6



authors list the study of bisimulation of graphs as future work. The dynamics paper
calls a ﬁxed pointed weighted multigraph special when, for every well-founded la-
beling, the decoration of the point uniquely determines the entire decoration on that
graph, and it gives examples of special and non-special graphs [3, Deﬁnition 5.3 and
Section 5.2]. This concerns recovery of the full decoration with the graph held ﬁxed,
and not reconstruction of arbitrary topology from a thema. Whenever distinct full
decorations on a ﬁxed graph share a thema, the same thematic state can correspond
to different underlying states. This non-uniqueness does not by itself establish a fail-
ure of dynamical closure. Closure fails only if two such states yield different thematic
states after an update, so the question is whether the distinctions lost in passing to the
thema can affect its continuation, and not whether the full graph can be reconstructed.

A small example separates the two. Let full states be pairs (x, y), let π(x, y) = x, and
compare the updates

                        S1(x, y) = (x, 0),     S2(x, y) = (y, 0).

The projection is many-to-one in both cases. Under S1 it is closed, with F(x) = x.
Under S2 it is not closed whenever different values of y occur with the same x, because
πS2(x, y) = y is not a function of x. An injective projection is trivially closed, but
injectivity is not necessary for closure.

This yields a question the paper leaves open and the closure condition makes precise.
For which networks, and for which choices of distinguished node, is the projection to
the thema closed under the dynamics? Where it is closed, the thematic level can be
studied as a dynamical system in its own right. Where it is not, any description at that
level is incomplete in a speciﬁc and measurable way, since the missing information is
exactly what separates states that the viewpoint cannot tell apart but the future can.


5. THE CONSCIOUSNESS OPERATORS

The paper interprets a class of operators K as consciousness operators, subject to four
axioms:

        Kx ⊆x,    x /∈Kx,    Kx /∈x,    x ⊆y =⇒Kx = x ∩Ky.


The authors name them Generation, Irreversibility, Removal, and Selection, and read
them as conditions relating a primary experience x, modeled as a set, to the awareness
Kx it induces [2]. Their semantic thesis is that consciousness is the result of such
an operator acting on experience, and their central example is the Russell operator
Rx = { y ∈x  | y /∈y }, which they show satisﬁes all four axioms. The axioms
are deﬁnite mathematical restrictions, and it is worth seeing what they impose before
asking what they mean.

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                      7


The last axiom has a revealing consequence. Taking {a} ⊆x gives

                            K({a}) = {a} ∩Kx,


so whether a is selected is settled by how the operator treats its singleton, indepen-
dently of which larger set contains it. At this level K behaves as a ﬁxed element-
selection criterion. The foundations paper proves a stronger form of the point: an
operator satisfying the fourth axiom is determined entirely by its action on single-
tons, through Kx = { y ∈x  | K{y} = {y} }, and two such operators compose by
intersection, so that K2 = K and consciousness operators commute [2]. Applying
a single operator a second time therefore changes nothing, and composing several
yields their intersection. The selector W of Section 2 is an operator of the same kind,
being selection by the predicate of being well-founded, and it satisﬁes all four axioms.
The ﬁrst is immediate, and the fourth holds because selection by any predicate sat-
isﬁes x ⊆y ⇒Wx = x ∩Wy, as the foundations paper notes for operators of this
form [2]. For the second, if x ∈Wx, then x is well-founded, since W keeps only well-
founded sets, and x ∈x, which is impossible. For the third, if Wx ∈x, then Wx, a
set all of whose elements are well-founded, is itself well-founded and so belongs to
Wx, which is again impossible. Relations among elements can already be encoded
inside the elements themselves, but the operator does not vary its selection with the
surrounding context. That makes it hard to identify the operator with attention or
awareness, both of which are usually taken to depend on context, unless some fur-
ther account of that dependence is supplied.

More generally, the axioms contain no independent condition that separates con-
scious from unconscious activity, no way to pick out a particular sensory quality, and
no route to predicting a report of experience. The paper attaches semantic readings to
its objects, and those readings are interpretations. Before the construction can count
as an explanatory theory of consciousness it needs an empirical bridge, a speciﬁed
correspondence between its objects and something observable, and the axioms do
not provide one. The authors state that they do not claim a complete characterization
of consciousness and present the approach as a way of introducing awareness into
a theory [2], so the observation here is only that the axioms alone do not supply the
bridge. The closure condition from Section 4 is the part of the framework that does
not depend on the interpretation, since it can be stated and tested for any projection
of any system.


6. SUBJECTIVITY AS A METHOD

A methodological move common in philosophy of mind deﬁnes the object of study as
whatever is available from a point of view, and treats everything the viewpoint does
not contain as outside the subject matter. In the vocabulary of this essay, a point of
view is a projection. The thema is the paper’s version of one: the state of the whole

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                      8



network as seen from a single node. The move has a cost that is easy to overlook. If
whatever the projection retains is called experience and whatever it discards is called
non-experience, then no result can ever count against the identiﬁcation, because every
discrepancy is reclassiﬁed as lying outside the viewpoint. A claim protected in this
way has no content as an empirical claim, however natural it feels as a description.

The closure condition restores content. Whether a ﬁrst-person description is an au-
tonomous level of explanation becomes a question with a determinate answer: do
states that look the same from the viewpoint remain the same after the system up-
dates? When πS = Fπ holds, the viewpoint is dynamically closed, its states evolve
according to a rule stated entirely in its own terms, and the subjective level can be
studied on its own. When the condition fails, the same thematic state has different
futures, and any description conﬁned to the viewpoint depends on hidden informa-
tion to continue. The refusal to answer for what lies outside a point of view, which
philosophers adopt as a policy, is thereby turned into a statement about when the
outside can safely be ignored.

This also clariﬁes why mathematical formulation has long served as a device for man-
aging the difﬁculties of subjectivity. A structural result can be stated without reference
to any individual, anecdote, or named case, and can be checked by anyone, which is
what objectivity amounts to in practice: independence from who is making the claim.
The qualiﬁcation is that this covers the proofs and not the modeling choices that pre-
cede them. Deciding that the decoration at a node is the object to be called experience,
or that one projection rather than another is the relevant one, is a choice made un-
der assumptions and interests, and a formalism can hide such a choice by making its
consequences look inevitable. A disciplined treatment therefore states the structural
results in full generality and marks each point at which an interpretation is added,
naming the node, the projection, and the label as separate decisions that each need
their own defense.


7. SELECTION BY SUFFICIENCY

The closure condition applies to any mechanism that selects which features of a sys-
tem are retained, not only to the particular projection studied above. Let σ be a selec-
tion that maps states to retained features, and let T be a family of operations that the
retained features will be used to anticipate or perform. Say that σ is sufﬁcient for T  if it
is closed under every operation in the family, in the sense of Section 4: for each S ∈T ,
states that agree under σ agree after S. A sufﬁcient selection is one whose discarded
distinctions cannot alter any outcome the family cares about.  It is relative to T , so
a selection can be sufﬁcient for one family of operations and insufﬁcient for another,
and the question of adequacy cannot be asked without naming the operations.

The requirement can also be relaxed to what is actually observed.  If o is an output
map naming what is read off after an operation, say that σ is sufﬁcient for (T , o)

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                      9


when σ(µ1) = σ(µ2) implies o(Sµ1) = o(Sµ2) for every S ∈T . This asks that the
observable result be reproduced without requiring that the retained features predict
the entire subsequent state. Closure together with the requirement that o be deter-
mined by σ implies this condition, but the condition does not imply closure, since
the retained features may fail to predict their own later values while still ﬁxing the
observed output.

A second kind of selection is governed by a ranking that does not refer to T at all,
such as a ranking by salience that retains whatever has most strongly drawn atten-
tion. Nothing in the ranking itself guarantees closure under the operations of interest.
A ranking can correlate reliably with task-relevant distinctions, through training, evo-
lution, or environmental regularity, and then closure may hold, but that alignment
is a further fact that needs its own support. A selection tuned to salience alone can
discard exactly the distinctions that continuation depends on. The contrast, stated in
these terms, is between selection that is established to be sufﬁcient for the tasks at
hand and selection that supplies no such guarantee, and it can be examined as a prop-
erty of projections without reference to any particular system in which either occurs.
Applied to the construction of Sections 1 to 4, the question is whether the thema pro-
jection is sufﬁcient for the dynamics, which is the closure condition of Section 4 read
as a sufﬁciency claim. The ranking case corresponds to the situation in which the pro-
jection is ﬁxed by something other than the dynamics it will be used to predict, and
sufﬁciency is then a further fact that needs its own support.

A recent case from machine learning shows the distinction operating in practice [8]. In
sequential state tracking on ﬁve boxes, the state after k moves is an arrangement of the
objects, and the arrangement after move k + 1 is ﬁxed by the arrangement after move k
together with that move. The arrangement is therefore a selection that is sufﬁcient, in
the sense above, for the family of single moves, although it discards nearly everything
a hidden state of a language model could carry. Wang and colleagues train a weight-
tied looped language model so that iteration k reports the arrangement after k moves,
and they ﬁnd that extrapolation to longer sequences depends on two conditions: each
iteration must be supervised with the arrangement it is meant to hold, and the scale
of the recurrent state must be held ﬁxed so that the step map is the same function at
every iteration. In their controlled ablations, removing the norm anchoring reduced
extrapolation from sixteen times the training length to below about two and a quarter
times, and replacing the arrangement targets with ﬁnal-answer supervision reduced
it to at most eight times. The reading offered here is this essay’s and not the authors’,
who do not use its vocabulary. Supervising the ﬁnal answer at every iteration asks an
intermediate state to determine something it does not yet contain, and a drifting scale
means that the projected update is no longer a single map F. The case also marks
a difference from the construction studied above. For Miranker and Zuckerman the
projection is ﬁxed by the representation and closure is a fact to be tested, whereas in

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                     10



the trained model the projection is shaped to be sufﬁcient and closure is secured by
training and not discovered. The results are those of a single preprint on synthetic
tasks, and they illustrate the sufﬁciency condition without testing anything about the
thema.


8. LIMITS

Several things the construction does not show should be stated plainly.  It adds no
causal mechanism to the underlying network. The set-based description evolves con-
sistently with the threshold dynamics, as Section 3 argues, but a consistent redescrip-
tion is not a new cause. It also does not establish an ontological division. The foun-
dations paper separates physical neural states, which can be observed and measured,
from the sets decorating their graphs, which it treats as Platonic and located in a vir-
tual space. The mathematical distinction is real, but treating one side as physical and
the other as virtual is an interpretation added to it, and a difference between math-
ematical representations does not establish a corresponding difference in what they
represent. Circular sets can encode recurrence without recurrence thereby becoming
experience.

There is also a computational qualiﬁcation. The foundations paper observes that anti-
foundation guarantees the existence of a decoration without giving a method for con-
structing it by recursion, and takes the resulting failure of effective construction to re-
inforce the Platonic status of the decorations [2]. This should be read narrowly, since
what fails is the unfolding of a circular set into an explicit well-founded membership
structure, and not the ﬁnite speciﬁcation of the graph and its decoration. Failure of or-
dinary well-founded recursive evaluation does not imply that ﬁnite cyclic structures
cannot be represented and manipulated by computation. A ﬁnite graph speciﬁes a
circular set without any algorithm having to unfold its full membership structure,
and for ﬁnite graphs whose labels have ﬁnite membership representations, including
the rational-weight histograms considered here, the question of whether two pointed
graphs have the same decoration reduces to bisimilarity of the associated expanded
membership graphs of Section 4, which is decidable by partition reﬁnement [7]. The
choice of anti-foundation therefore does not by itself demonstrate a capacity beyond
ﬁnite graph processing, and the non-computability of the unfolded sets does not by
itself support placing them outside the physical description.

Finally, the closure condition is a statement about a projection and a dynamics, and
its verdicts are only as good as the model supplied.  It says whether a viewpoint
determines its own continuation within the model. Whether the model corresponds
to anything beyond itself is a separate question that the formalism leaves open, and
the open question about which networks and which distinguished nodes satisfy the
condition remains the most direct place for the construction to be tested.

CLOSURE UNDER PROJECTION                                                     11
